7a7be8479fff: You cannot tell the story of this family properly by following the surnames. Do that, and you get a string of changing names — Jensen, Thomsen, Madsen, Mikkelsen — and lose the thread at the first bend.
d1c195b19e3e: The thread is Silkjær, and it runs through both sexes and every branch.
e7702270b309: made the farm name the family’s — the children bore it in the census of 1890, and in 1905 he received a name certificate for it.

7b8cc18bef42: Three cousins, six years, the same choice
c870d03de375: Three sisters from Økjær. Three different husbands, three different surnames, three different parishes. And within six years all three call their son <t1>Niels Silkjær</t1> — named after their father, with the farm’s name fixed in the middle. No document tells us they had agreed on it. Yet the pattern is so clear that the choices of name were hardly a coincidence.
55a6786638c5: The men carried the name on because they kept it. Through the women it was carried on <t1>even though</t1> they lost it as a surname at their wedding: at the baptisms, Silkjær was written into the next generation.
270aaadecbbe: Of Niels Thomsen’s daughters, five passed the name on to their children: Ane Marie, Ane Johanne, Karen Marie, Ane Kirstine and Ellen. In the next generation Laura and Elna Elisabeth, among others, did the same.
ceb2dcae0aa8: The family lived in a time of transition, when place name, byname, middle name and surname overlapped. The same person can appear in the sources as Thomsen, as Nielsen Silkjær or simply as Silkjær — and that is not muddle. It is the naming culture itself. Nor was the custom the family’s own: the fishing family in Esbjerg that Kristine Oline married into in 1916 likewise used a byname as a middle name before it became a fixed surname — Højberg carried in the middle of the name, unevenly shared among the sons, and in 1930 made a surname by royal licence, twenty-five years after Niels Thomsen’s name certificate. [S75, S76] What is remarkable is not that the name changed place. It is that it stayed there.
47cd48a7fe2e: Today Silkjær is once again borne as a surname in the Mikkelsen line — by the children and grandchildren of Laura’s youngest son, Leif, born in 1956. And they are not alone: the name lives on in other branches of the family, where it never had time to disappear.
fdf54bbfc2d6: And the name did not travel only across the map. The story began among copyhold farmers and smallholders who launched open boats from the beach — and within a few generations the family included fishing skippers with cutters of their own, a chairman of a parish council, an accountant with his own office on the harbour and a chief clerk who ended up owning a mineral-water factory. None of them did anything out of the ordinary; they did what the century made possible. It was not one straight climb, and the branches went different ways. But laid end to end, the lives show how much the society around the name had changed.
e2e93e24ee45: And the name stayed where it came from. In a school photograph from Husby in 1960 a boy is noted as “Kurt Pedersen (Silkjær)”. His name was Pedersen, and his family had taken over the farm long after the Silkjærs had moved away; the parish still knew him by the name of the place. So Silkjær existed as a place name before there was a family of that name — and went on existing in the place after the family had taken it with them out into the country. [S115]
b095368f68d3: The circle is not quite closed; circles of this kind never close entirely. None of the living has lived on the farm, and most have never worked at sea. But the name stands where it stood with Niels Thomsen a good hundred and forty years ago: as the family’s.
beeadeff92b2:
It began as a description of a wet piece of land in Husby parish.
It became a man.
It became a family.
And it became what a family chose to remember — every single time they had the chance not to.
d0076cf5ae81: The descendants can still stand on the land the name came from. But they stand there as guests.
